newsitem.title: INDIA: India coalition cements divide, ends crisis.
newsitem.headline: India coalition cements divide, ends crisis.

text.p: India's shaky centre-left coalition overcame a four-day-long crisis on Thursday when a regional party backed off from a threat to quit Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's government.

The crisis blew over after leaders of the 15-party United Front agreed in a four-hour meeting that its squabbles could only help rival Hindu nationalists waiting to grab chances in a likely mid-term election, alliance leaders said.

The Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) party decided not to press its threat to withdraw its four ministers because it was upset with some coalition partners, Information and Broadcasting Minister Jaipal Reddy told reporters.
"I would say the problem is over," Reddy said.

The United Front has 178 lawmakers in the parliament's 545-member lower house and gets vital support for its minority rule from the Congress party, which has 140 deputies. Congress itself was thrown out of power in elections in 1996.
The coalition is ranged against the Hindu BJP which controls 193 votes. Opinion polls indicate the BJP would stand a good chance of capturing power if a mid-term election were held now.

The DMK, sinking differences with communist partners, also endorsed a decision by the United Front not to admit a breakaway group of Gujral's Janata Dal party, the Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD), alliance leaders said.
"This is a compromise that was arrived at after all the deliberations," said a leader who asked not to be identified.
DMK leaders said earlier this week they did not like the hard line of the Communist Party of India-Marxist (CPI-M), one of the alliance members, that the RJD must not be admitted to the ruling bloc.

"DMK has been of the view that we should not do anything that will precipitate elections as the only beneficiary of a snap poll will be the BJP," a senior coalition leader said, referring to the opposition Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
The crisis was triggered earlier this month by a split in Gujral's Janata Dal party. It was compounded by a corruption scandal involving the politician who caused the split.
Indian markets were anxiously watching the political crisis. The key Bombay 30-share index closed 10.19 points higher at 4,193.61 on Thursday, breaking a five-day slide.
Gujral, who heads a two-month-old cabinet, is being accused by critics of lack of control over his squabbling partners in the coalition formed after elections last year.

The communists wanted Gujral to bar the RJD from the coalition because its leader, Laloo Prasad Yadav, has refused to resign as the chief minister of Bihar state after federal police indicted him in a corruption scandal.
The DMK threatened to pull out from the government on Monday, saying the communists were overstepping their limit by interfering in the affairs of Gujral's party.

Yadav said he was innocent in the $280 million scandal involving state animal welfare funds. He broke away from Gujral's Janata Dal on July 5 to set up the RJD, citing differences over an election for the party's top post.

But a big question mark hung over the future of three ministers in Gujral's government who belong to the RJD. Reddy said senior leaders did not take a decision on the issue, and could consider it at their next meeting on July 25.
